stances_toward.note: The Malvinas claim: Argentina claims the islands, which Britain controls. The claim dates back to 1833; 1982 (the war) is the sourced date here, not the start of the claim. Milei reaffirmed it in 2026 and London says sovereignty is not up for negotiation (99.8% of islanders voted to remain British in 2013, per the GBR card). Bond - grievance: the 1982 war. Added 2026-10-16: the economic stake is the licence regime - the Falklands fishery earned GBP 30.5m of licence fees in 2022 and is over 60% of the islands' GDP (Eurofish, 2023; no 2025 figure found), the individual transferable quotas were issued in 2022 for 25 years from 2023, and the Sea Lion field (Navitas 65%, Rockhopper the rest, first oil planned 2028, phase 1 at 50,000 b/d) is the new front. Stable: the claim has not moved, only its instruments.

relations_to.summary: Argentina claims the Falklands/Malvinas. Milei reaffirmed the claim in April 2026 and at the UN in September 2026, and said in December 2025 that arms-export talks with London had begun, which the Foreign Office denied; London says sovereignty is not up for negotiation.

relations_to.summary: The fisheries side of the claim. The Falklands fishery earned GBP 30.5m of licence fees in 2022 and accounts for over 60% of the islands' GDP (Eurofish, 2023; no 2025 figure found); the fisheries director issued individual transferable quotas in a resolution of 31 May 2022 for 25 years from 1 January 2023 (so to 2047), to companies flagged in Spain, South Korea, Vanuatu and the UK, which Argentine commentary calls illegal under Law 26,659. Taiwan-flagged squid fleets have not accepted British licensing since 2010. The ITQs are the economic anchor that makes the Sea Lion oil case a second front rather than the first.
